question.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
question.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }$, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta })^{2} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta }) \\  & =3\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta ) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt[3]{\operatorname{cos}⁡3\theta })^{2}+{(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }+\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{4}⁡3\theta }}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡3\theta }{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{4}⁡3\theta }}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{{cos}^{2}⁡3\theta }}\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\theta +\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ]}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{1}{2}-(-\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\frac{2+\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$
